title: Labour Overtakes Reform UK in Polls as Andy Burnham's 'Bounce' Reshapes British Politics
excerpt: Three separate polls show Labour pulling ahead of Nigel Farage's Reform UK for the first time in over a year, driven by a surge in young voters and the new prime minister's cost-of-living measures.
body:
• Three polls — by Survation, More In Common, and YouGov — show Labour overtaking or drawing level with Reform UK for the first time since early 2025, following Andy Burnham's appointment as prime minister on July 20.
  • Labour rose to 26-28 per cent in different polls while Reform dropped to 22-24 per cent, with Burnham's cost-of-living measures credited for the shift.
  • Young voters drove much of the swing: Labour's share among 18-to-24-year-olds jumped from 14 per cent to 26 per cent, while Green Party support in the same demographic dropped 20 points.
  • Reform UK has faced negative headlines over undeclared gifts, a convicted fraudster serving as an adviser, and a Metropolitan Police investigation into party payments.

The Burnham Bounce

For the first time in over a year, Britain's governing Labour Party has overtaken Nigel Farage's populist Reform UK in national opinion polls — a dramatic reversal that pollsters are calling the "Burnham bounce."

Three separate surveys released in late July show the shift. Survation put Labour at 26 per cent and Reform at 24 per cent. More In Common showed a wider gap, with Labour at 28 per cent against Reform's 24 per cent. YouGov had the two parties tied at 22 per cent, with Labour up six points since May and Reform at their lowest level since March 2025.

The turnaround follows Labour's decision to replace the deeply unpopular Keir Starmer with Andy Burnham, the charismatic former Mayor of Greater Manchester, who became prime minister on July 20. Reform had led nearly every opinion poll for more than a year and gained hundreds of seats in local and regional votes in May, making Starmer's position untenable.

Cost-of-Living Quick Wins

Burnham spent his first week in office focused on what his team called "breathing space" measures for voters struggling with the cost of living. The package included removing a tax on energy bills, capping bus fares, and cutting taxes for pubs and bars — modest but heavily promoted measures that appear to have connected with a broad spectrum of voters.

"I won't get carried away, but I'm pleased to have made a start where hopefully I've connected with people."

— Andy Burnham, UK Prime Minister

YouGov found that 44 per cent of voters considered Burnham likeable, while 35 per cent thought he had the right ideas for the country. In head-to-head comparisons, Burnham beats every other party leader as preferred prime minister, leading Farage by a margin of 48 per cent to 22 per cent.

Young Voters Return to Labour

The most striking element of the poll data is the swing among young voters. In June, just 14 per cent of 18-to-24-year-olds said they would vote Labour. That figure has jumped to 26 per cent under Burnham. The rise came almost entirely at the expense of the Green Party, whose support among the youngest cohort plummeted from 46 per cent to 26 per cent in a single month.

The Times reported that the bounce was expected to translate into a comfortable victory for Bev Craig, Labour's candidate to succeed Burnham as Greater Manchester mayor, over Reform's Sian Astley. A More In Common poll suggested Craig would win 65 per cent to 35 per cent once second preferences were counted.

Reform Under Pressure

While Labour enjoys its bounce, Reform has faced a series of damaging revelations. Allegations that gifts and donations from wealthy backers were not properly declared have triggered scrutiny from the parliamentary standards watchdog. Reports of a convicted fraudster serving as a party adviser and a Metropolitan Police investigation into party payments have compounded the damage.

Farage, who resigned his seat in Clacton to trigger a by-election, has angrily dismissed the allegations as an establishment plot to discredit him, but the controversies appear to be eroding his party's polling numbers.

What It Means for the Indian Community in the UK

The political shift in Britain carries particular significance for the UK's 1.8 million-strong Indian-origin community. Labour's return to competitiveness could shape policy on immigration, trade ties with India, and the proposed India-UK free trade agreement that has stalled in recent years. Burnham's approach to the cost of living — including energy and transport costs — also resonates with British Indian households, many of whom are concentrated in constituencies where Labour and Reform are directly competing.
